column1: # G2: the validation verb (docs/capability-review/g2-validation-verb.md).
# Columns: name<TAB>vet<TAB>schema<TAB>data<TAB>expect
# FIVE columns, not four. Both runners read the first four columns of
# every other mode and ignore the rest, so a `vet` arm reading a fifth
# is additive rather than a format change. The alternative -- packing
# two documents into the single src cell with a separator -- founders on
# the same rock as a compact finding summary: no punctuation is safe,
# because a quoted map key may contain any character (see
# vet-path-with-space).
# `expect` is the report as a JSON object, compared through the
# serialiser pair the suite already holds to byte parity (exactJSON /
# json.Encoder), so key order and spacing in the cell do not matter --
# both sides are re-emitted before the comparison.
# MESSAGE TEXT IS EXCLUDED from the golden, deliberately. Codes are
# contractual across the ports and prose is not -- both runners say so
# at the `errc` site, and test/spec/divergent.tsv repeats it -- so a
# whole-report golden would silently promote every message string to a
# cross-port contract this repository refuses to make. The `message`
# field is asserted per port instead (ts/test/vet.test.ts, go/vet_test.go).
# OPTIONS ride in the expect object under an `opts` key, which the
# runners lift out before comparing. The engine takes options as an
# argument, and a sixth column for something a minority of rows use
# would be a worse trade than one reserved key in a cell that is
# already JSON.
# The two documents are named `schema` and `data` by the runner, not by
# a path, so the goldens do not depend on where the suite is checked out.
# The two negative verdicts are the mechanical answer to error.tsv's
# conflation: a contradiction can never be satisfied, incompleteness
# merely is not satisfied YET. Bare vet is strict about residue;
# --partial opts out of that without hiding the finding.
vet-valid
vet-invalid-kind
vet-incomplete
vet-partial-allows-residue
vet-conflict-outranks-residue
# A schema that does not stand up on its own is never blamed on data:
# verdict `error`, which is what the exit table means by exit 4. A DATA
# document that will not parse is the DATA's fault, so it is `invalid`
# with a finding carrying the parser's own code -- the same answer the
# engine already gave one character earlier, where a refused construct
# (vet-refused-construct below) reaches the tree as an ordinary nil.
# THE VERDICT IS NOT THE WHOLE REPORT. Every row below carries a
# finding, and the four of them pin the pairing the two halves of that
# sentence make: the verdict says WHOSE fault it is (`error` for the
# schema, `invalid` for the data) and the finding says WHAT and WHERE,
# in the same shape whichever document is at fault. Both ports used to
# answer a broken schema with an empty finding list, so a caller was
# told the schema did not stand up and never where it fell over -- the
# one report a repair loop can do nothing with.
# The sites are the FAILURE'S OPERANDS, and they name the schema
# because the provenance walk reaches them (ts/src/walk.ts,
# go/walk.go): a nil's operands are off-peg, exactly as a preference's
# yardstick is, and a walk that stopped at the nil left them anonymous.
vet-schema-error
vet-schema-error-nested
vet-data-unparseable
vet-data-merge-conflict
vet-schema-unparseable
vet-schema-merge-conflict
# The data site is listed first: it is the thing to fix. Roles come from
# provenance, not from NilVal's primary/secondary heuristic, which is
# source-order reasoning within ONE document and says nothing useful
# when one side is a schema and the other is data.
# The second row is the design's own motivating example: a parent that
# collapses to a nil takes its subtree with it, so one finding stands in
# the tree and the other is only on the context. Both are reported.
vet-closed-key
vet-closed-key-and-conflict
# expected/actual come from the constraint algebra's own details, so
# G1's canonical bound syntax is what a repair loop is handed, and the
# author's message from Band B rides the finding as `note`.
vet-constraint-alternatives
vet-must-note
# A path is not delimiter-safe, which is why the whole finding list is
# JSON rather than a compact code@path summary. The empty key is the
# sharpest case: the machine-readable path keeps the segment, while the
# message drops it (val.go, messagePath).
vet-path-with-space
vet-path-empty-key
vet-root-conflict
# A list peg is an array and a map peg an object: the walk follows both,
# and a spread template lives off-peg again. Note WHERE the spread
# finding lands -- the path is the TEMPLATE's, because the conflict is
# created against the template node; the data site still points at the
# offending value, which is what a repair loop needs.
vet-list-index
vet-list-two-conflicts
vet-spread-template
# SITES. A failure raised about a construct rather than a failed meet
# carries no operands, and is reported about itself. A JUNCTION NOW
# REPORTS ITS OWN POSITION: the meet mints a fresh disjunction, which
# used to arrive unsited, so every finding naming a disjunction that had
# met anything pointed at -1:-1 with no file and an agent reading the
# report had nowhere to go (the review's finding F). The narrowed
# disjunction now carries the site of the one it came from -- the
# parser does give a junction a position, the start of its first
# alternative -- so the row below is the site the schema text has. A
# preference's synthesised type yardstick
# lives OFF-PEG, so provenance reaches it only because the stamp walk
# follows superpeg deliberately -- without that it belonged to neither
# document, and the two ports disagreed about which. The yardstick it
# reports is the preferred value's own KIND (`integer` for `*1`); it
# read `number` until the family gate was removed on 2026-08-25. Columns
# count UTF-16 code units, as the canonical port's sites do.
vet-operandless-nil
vet-refused-construct
vet-junction-site
# ... AND A JUNCTION REACHED THROUGH A REFERENCE keeps it, which is
# the shape a schema actually has: an enum is declared once and named
# from wherever it applies. Resolving the reference CLONES the
# disjunction, and the Go clone rebuilt it as a fresh value carrying
# the url and the text but not the position -- so this finding pointed
# at row -1 there and at the enum here (the "junction values at -1:-1"
# half of the review's finding F). The site travels whole now.
vet-refd-disjunct-site
vet-pref-yardstick
# A value the engine mints for ITSELF belongs to neither document, and
# says so with an empty file rather than borrowing one: an unknown var
# meets `top`, which no parser sited and no stamp walk reached. Both
# ports leave the name empty, so the emptiness is the contract -- a
# port that quietly labelled it `schema` would be claiming the mistake
# is in a document the reader can open and look at.
vet-unstamped-operand
vet-utf16-column
vet-utf16-astral
# The data document is PARSED and not evaluated before it meets the
# schema, so anything the grammar builds is still standing when
# provenance is stamped: a function call, a `+` operator, a constraint
# with its arguments. The stamp walk has to follow all of them, or a
# site inside one is labelled as coming from the wrong document.
vet-data-function
vet-data-operator
vet-data-constraint
vet-data-pending-constraint
# Vet sorts its own findings. The underlying walk follows raw key order
# and the two hosts disagree about that, so an unsorted report could
# never be in cross-port parity. Truncation is declared, never silent.
vet-sorted-by-data-site
vet-truncated
# `--at` validates against a subtree of the schema, `--closed` closes
# THAT anchor (a scalar anchor has no keys, so the flag is inert), and
# an anchor that is not there is an error verdict rather than a pass --
# WITH the refusal `get` and `why` give for a path that names nothing,
# `no_path`, down to the "did you mean" (excluded from the golden with
# every other message). Exit 4 and an empty finding list left the
# caller nothing to act on, which is the whole complaint the `error`
# verdict's other rows answer.
vet-at-subtree
vet-at-bare-path
vet-at-list-index
vet-at-missing
vet-at-through-scalar
# `--closed` on a LIST schema, unanchored: the flag seals the anchor
# whatever kind of bag it is, so a surplus ELEMENT is refused the way a
# surplus key is. (The anchored list case is vet-at-list-index above.)
vet-closed-list-surplus
vet-closed-list-exact
# A SCHEMA-INTERNAL REFERENCE SEES THE DATA (ADR-007,
# use-cases/BUGS.md §15). `b:$.a` used to be resolved and REPLACED by
# the standalone pass, which decides whether the schema stands up on
# its own -- and that settled tree was then the left side of the meet,
# so `{a:3,b:4}` vetted valid while the same four lines as one document
# refuse with scalar_value. Both sites are in the DATA, because both
# values the meet could not reconcile were written there: the reference
# contributes the path, not a value.
vet-schema-reference-sees-data
vet-schema-reference-agrees
# THE MEET IS FROM A FRESH PARSE, EXCEPT UNDER `--at` (ADR-007). An
# unanchored run meets the schema as PARSED, so its references see the
# data -- that is what makes vet(S,D) and eval(S u D) the same question
# (use-cases/BUGS.md §15). An anchor is a SUBTREE lifted out of the
# schema, and an absolute reference inside it names a sibling of the
# document ROOT, which the lifted subtree no longer has; the settled
# tree is where such a reference has already been resolved and
# substituted, so an anchored run keeps meeting that. These rows pin
# the anchored side of the rule: the reference's contribution is still
# enforced, in both ports.
vet-at-absolute-ref-valid
vet-at-absolute-ref-invalid
# A MARK ABOVE THE ANCHOR IS NOT A REASON TO CHECK NOTHING (ADR-007's
# companion, the completeness probe -- use-cases/BUGS.md §14). Vet finds
# residue by GENERATING the anchored meet, and generation honours the
# output marks: `type()` and `hide()` say "do not emit this". So a
# `--at` anchor sitting under a `type()` -- the ordinary way a schema
# names a reusable definition -- generated nothing, reported nothing,
# and vetted VALID for data missing a required key, while the same
# anchor without the mark answered incomplete. A mark is a decision
# about OUTPUT, and `--at` names the truth to validate against
# explicitly; the probe now descends through it. The conflict row is
# the control: wrong-KIND values were always refused, so a fix that
# merely reported more would not be visible there.
vet-at-marked-anchor-required
vet-at-marked-anchor-complete
vet-at-marked-anchor-conflict
# A MISSING REQUIRED ENUM FIELD IS INCOMPLETE, NOT VALID (ADR-007,
# use-cases/BUGS.md §13). Generation used to FOLD an unresolved
# disjunction's members together with unify, so `'a'|'b'` with no data
# died as a scalar CONFLICT -- the conflict of the fold, not of anything
# the author wrote -- and the incompleteness pass, which keeps
# incomplete-class findings, filtered it out. Verdict: valid, zero
# findings, for the commonest schema idiom there is. The other two rows
# are the controls at either end: a value that selects an alternative
# passes, one that selects none is still the empty-disjunct refusal.
# The schema site is (-1,-1): a disjunction spans its members and
# carries no source position of its own. Pinned as it stands rather
# than papered over -- it is the review's finding F, open in both ports.
vet-enum-missing-is-incomplete
vet-enum-member-is-valid
vet-enum-non-member-is-invalid
# AN ANCHOR IS A STRUCTURAL PATH -- map keys and list indices, and
# nothing else. Reading it off whatever a value's peg happened to hold
# walked into a junction's branches, a constraint's own arguments, and
# an array's `length`, which handed back a JavaScript number as the
# anchor and made every document valid.
vet-at-through-junction
vet-at-through-constraint
vet-at-list-length
vet-closed-anchor
vet-closed-scalar-anchor-inert
# --- multi-error collection (G2 phase 6) ------------------------------
# The pass loop continues past an erroring pass, so a failure only a
# LATER pass can reach is collected in the same run (the second row's
# $.b.p used to surface as a vague unsited incompleteness). What keeps
# the report from cascading: a nil is ABSORBING in the engine, and the
# report dedups by (code, sites) -- NOT (code, path), because a
# reference resolves by cloning its target, so one failed target can
# fail once per referrer with a different path each time. One cause,
# one finding: the fan-in and cycle rows pin the collapse (the cycle
# used to report twice even under the single-pass loop).
multi-second-pass-conflict
multi-fanin-one-finding
multi-spread-children
multi-cycle-one-finding
# A NEGATIVE LITERAL and an OVERFLOWING one, here for their SITE SPANS
# rather than their verdicts. Both were parity gaps no other row could
# see: Go stamped the source span on a refused negation but not on a
# successful one, and both of its overflow refusals returned before the
# stamp -- so `a:-1` and `a:1e999` reported `len:-1, src:""` where the
# canonical port reported the `-` token and the literal. Found in review
# of the Site-extent change; a green suite over a real divergence is
# exactly what a shared row is for.
vet-negative-literal
vet-overflow-literal
# A VALUE UNIFICATION MINTED IS UNSITED, and says so with -1 rather than
# claiming a position. `a: 1+2` contributes the RESULT 3, which no
# author wrote and which is therefore nowhere in particular.
# Found by the parity probe for `set --in-place` and fixed rather than
# recorded, the G2 phase-4 pattern: Go reported these at row 1 column 1
# -- a real place, and the wrong one -- because `sp`'s zero value IS a
# position (the first byte), so an unstamped value was indistinguishable
# from one written at the very start of the document. Go's junctions had
# always set `sp = -1` explicitly for exactly this reason; the scalar
# minters never did. siteOf already guarded on `0 <= v.pos()` and needed
# no change: it was being handed a position that looked real.
vet-minted-arith-operand-unsited
vet-minted-concat-operand-unsited
# THE ADMISSION GATE UNDER VET (ADR-004, 2026-08-26; use-cases/BUGS.md
# §1). The enum-with-default schema now refuses an out-of-enum data
# value: `k:*'auto'|'literal'|'data'` against `k:'autoo'` was
# `verdict: valid` (the same-kind override replaced the default with no
# alternative consulted), and is now the `|:empty` refusal, reported at
# the data site. A member value stays valid. The schema's own
# pref_not_instance warning rides along in both reports (the lint's
# post-gate advisory reading -- see ts/src/vet.ts). Parity-probed.
vet-enum-default-refuses-nonmember
vet-enum-default-admits-member
# Two unequal cross-statement spreads addressing one map at DIFFERENT
# depths (2026-08-26, the spread application rework; BUGS.md sec 7's
# vet form): vetting data that satisfies both templates is VALID --
# the historic crosswire reported one sibling's own value conflicting
# with another sibling's. Parity-probed.
vet-unequal-spread-depths
# A CONFLICT INSIDE A REFERENCED RECORD NAMES THE KEY, not the record
# (use-cases/BUGS.md §41). A value that arrives by reference is
# re-pathed to the referring field, and the operand path a nil used to
# take its own path from put every conflict in `q: $.M` at `$.q` -- the
# same path for every field of the record, so a repair loop was told to
# rewrite the whole thing, twice, instead of the two keys that clash.
# Both spellings of the alias, since only one of them carries a mark.
vet-ref-clone-names-the-key-not-the-record
vet-type-alias-names-the-key-not-the-record
